questions.question: Fatehabad district derives its name from the eponymous headquarters town founded by ______ in the 14 th century, who named it after his son Fateh Khan.
questions.questionHtml: Fatehabad district derives its name from the eponymous headquarters town founded by ______ in the 14<sup>th</sup> century, who named it after his son Fateh Khan.
questions.solution:
• Fatehabad district derives its name from the eponymous headquarters town founded by Firoz Shah Tughlaq in the 14th century, who named it after his son Fateh Khan. 
  • Firoz Shah was the third ruler of Tughlaq dynasty and he reigned from 1351 to 1388 AD.
  • He established the Diwan-i-Khairat, Diwan-i-Bundagan, Sarais (rest house) for the benefits of merchants and adopted the Iqtadari framework.
  • Firozabad, Fatehabad, Jaunpur and Hissar were established by him.
  • He also constructed various canals and imposed certain taxes.

questions.question: In which year was the Battle of Talikota fought between the Vijayanagara Empire and the Deccan sultanates?
questions.questionHtml: In which year was the Battle of Talikota fought between the Vijayanagara Empire and the Deccan sultanates?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 1565 AD.

  • Battle of Talikota, confrontation in the Deccan region of southern India between the forces of the Hindu raja of Vijayanagar and the four allied Muslim sultans of Bijapur, Bidar, Ahmadnagar, and Golconda.
    • The battle was fought in January, 1565, at a site southeast of Bijapur, in what is now northern Karnataka state.

Additional Information

  •  Krishna Deva Raya, king of the Vijaynagar empire at its zenith, stormed the Raichur Fort after a bloodily victorious battle against the forces of Ismail Adil Shah, ruler of the Bijapur Sultanate.
    • The Battle of Raichur (1520), though celebrated widely through the streets of Vijayanagara, signaled the slow-yet-steady downfall of the Vijayanagara Empire.
    • Ultimately, the Battle of Talikota (1565) brought about the fated decline of a kingdom over two hundred years old.
    • After this decisive battle, the Vijayanagara Empire could never reach the same heights of the past.

questions.question: Who became the Nawab of Bengal after the death of Alivardi Khan in 1756?

questions.question: Who among the following Sultans of Delhi established Turkan - i - Chahalgani?
questions.questionHtml: Who among the following Sultans of Delhi established Turkan - i - Chahalgani?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Iltumish .

Key Points

  • Iltumish (1211-1236):
    • ​He completed the famous Qutab Minar in Delhi.
    • He shifted his capital from Lahore to Delhi.
    • The Mongol policy of Iltutmish saved India from the wrath of Ghengis Khan.
    • ​He was the real founder of the Delhi sultanate.
    • He ruled from 1211 to 1236 AD.
    • He introduces the Iqta system and made it hereditary.
    • He also introduces Chalisa (a group of 40 noble people).
    • He introduces two coins:
      • Silver coin - Taka
      • Copper coin - Jital

 Additional Information

  • Ghiyasuddin Balban (1266-1287):
    • ​He was the greatest ruler of the Slave dynasty.
    • Balban started the rigorous court discipline and new customs called Paibos (prostration and kissing the Sultan's feet) to prove his superiority over the nobles.
    • He broke the power of forty, Turkish nobles, who were the real threat to the monarchy.
    • His tomb is located in Mehrauli, Delhi.
  • Bhalol Lodhi
    • Bahlul Lodi was a ruler of the Lodi dynasty who ruled from 1451 to 1489.
      • He is known for his military campaigns and expansion of the Lodi empire.
  • ​Alauddin Khilji
    • In 1296 A.D. Ala-ud-din Khilji succeeded Jalal-ud-din Firoz Khilji and ascended the throne.
    • Ala-ud-din Khilji Invasions in the North- captured Ranthambore and killed Hamir Deva its ruler and  also captured Malwa, Chittor, Dhar, Mandu, Ujjain, Marwar, Chanderi and Jalor.
    • Ala-ud-din Khilji Invasions in the South - was the first Sultan who attacked South India and sent general Malik Kafur against the rulers of the south. Prataprudra-II of Warangal, Ramachandra Deva, the Yadava king of Devagiri, and Vira Ballala-III the Hoysala king were defeated.
    • The domestic Policies of Alauddin Khilji Ala-ud-din followed -the Divine Right Theory of Kingship, introduced four ordinances to prevent repeated revolts; impounded pious grants and free grants of lands; restructured the spy system; banned social parties and wine; introduced a permanent standing army; started the system of branding of horses and a descriptive roster of individual soldiers to inhibit corruption; fixed the prices of necessary commodities which were below the normal market rates; strictly prohibited black marketing. Revenue was collected in cash and not in kind; followed discriminatory policies towards the Hindus and imposed the Jizya, a grazing tax and a house tax on the Hindu community.
    • He was the first to bring the standing army system.
    • He constructed Alai Darwaza, the Palace of a thousand pillars and the Fort of Siri.

questions.question: Vijay Stambh was built by which of these rulers?
questions.questionHtml: Vijay Stambh was built by which of these rulers?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Rana Kumbha.

Key Points

  • Vijay Stambha is an imposing victory monument located in Chittorgarh fort in Chittorgarh, Rajasthan.
  • It was constructed by Mewar king Rana Kumbha in 1448 to commemorate his victory over the combined armies of Malwa and Gujarat led by Mahmud Khilji.

Additional Information

  • Rana Kumbha (1417-1468)
    • Reign of Mewar: Rana Kumbha was a powerful ruler of the Mewar kingdom in Rajasthan, India, reigning from 1433 to 1468 CE.
    • Military Prowess: He was a renowned warrior who expanded the boundaries of Mewar through numerous successful military campaigns against neighboring kingdoms.
    • Architectural Patronage: Kumbha is celebrated for his significant contributions to architecture. He commissioned the construction of the magnificent Kumbhalgarh Fort, one of the most impregnable fortresses in India. He also patronized the building of numerous Hindu and Jain temples, showcasing intricate stone carvings and sculptures.
    • Cultural Patronage: Kumbha was a patron of arts and literature. He was himself a skilled musician and a scholar, contributing to the development of Indian classical music.
  • Durga Das Rathore (1638-1718)
    • Loyal General: Durga Das Rathore was a renowned Rajput general who served under several Mughal emperors, including Aurangzeb.
    • Master Strategist: He was known for his military brilliance and strategic acumen.
    • Champion of Rajput Pride: Despite serving the Mughals, Durga Das remained fiercely loyal to his Rajput heritage and often championed the cause of Rajput independence.
    • Key Role in Rajput Resistance: He played a crucial role in uniting Rajput clans against Mughal dominance, fostering a sense of collective resistance.
  • Maharana Pratap (1540-1597)
    • Ruler of Mewar: Maharana Pratap was a valiant ruler of Mewar who famously resisted Mughal emperor Akbar's attempts to conquer his kingdom.
    • Symbol of Rajput Resistance: He is a revered figure in Indian history, symbolizing Rajput valor and resistance against foreign rule.
    • The Battle of Haldighati: The Battle of Haldighati, fought between Pratap and Akbar's forces, is legendary. Though the outcome was inconclusive, Pratap's courage and resilience in the face of overwhelming odds have earned him legendary status.
    • Guerrilla Warfare: After the Battle of Haldighati, Pratap resorted to guerrilla warfare tactics to continue his resistance against the Mughals, effectively keeping them out of Mewar for much of his reign.
  • Prithvi Raj Chauhan (c. 1178-1192)
    • Last Hindu Shahi Ruler of Delhi and Ajmer: Prithvi Raj Chauhan was the last Hindu Shahi ruler of Delhi and Ajmer.
    • Conquest of Delhi: He succeeded in capturing Delhi from the Ghaznavids, restoring Hindu rule to the region.
    • Conflict with Muhammad Ghori: He engaged in a series of battles with the Afghan ruler Muhammad Ghori.

questions.question: The Khalji or Khilji dynasty, founded by Jalal-ud-din Firuz Khalji ruled large parts of the Indian subcontinent between ________.
questions.questionHtml: The Khalji or Khilji dynasty, founded by Jalal-ud-din Firuz Khalji ruled large parts of the Indian subcontinent between ________.

questions.question: The famous tripartite struggle was fought for control over ________ in early medieval period.
questions.questionHtml: The famous tripartite struggle was fought for control over ________ in early medieval period.
questions.solution: The Tripartite Struggle, commonly referred to as the Kannauj Triangle Wars, transpired in the ninth century, revolving around the battle for dominance in northern India among three prominent empires: the Gurjara-Pratihara Empire, the Pala Empire, and the Rashtrakuta Empire.

questions.question: Hamideh Banu Maryam Makani was the wife of Mughal emperor ______.
questions.questionHtml: Hamideh Banu Maryam Makani was the wife of Mughal emperor ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Humayun.

Key Points

  • Hamideh Banu Maryam Makani was the wife of Mughal emperor Humayun.
  • Hamida Banu Begum was chief and most favourite consort of the second Mughal emperor Humayun and the mother of his successor, the third Mughal emperor Akbar.
  • She is also known by the title Maryam Makani, which was given to her by her son, Akbar.

Additional Information

Tips to Remember: (BHAJSA) for chronological order.

B -> Babur

H -> Humayun

A -> Akbar

J -> Jahangir

S -> Shah Jahan

A -> Aurangzeb

questions.question: In which year was Battle of Peshawar fought between Raja Jayapal and Mahmud Ghazni?

questions.solution: The Battle of Peshawar was fought between Raja Jayapala and Mahmud of Ghazni in 1001 CE. Raja Jayapala was the ruler of the Hindu Shahi dynasty, while Mahmud of Ghazni was a prominent Muslim conqueror from the Ghaznavid dynasty.

questions.question: In the context of state and administration in the Delhi Sultanate, the term 'muqti' means:
questions.questionHtml: In the context of state and administration in the Delhi Sultanate, the term 'muqti' means:

options.text: the head of a village community
options.html: the head of a village community

options.text: the holder of a land assignment called 'iqta'
options.html: the holder of a land assignment called 'iqta'

questions.solution:
• Muqtis were commanders of military and administrative blocks known as iqta.
  • The Iqta system started with the need of early Turkish Sultans.
  • Those areas of the Sultanate located away from the capital, which was not easy for the revenue collection, was given as an Iqta by the Sultan.
  • The Iqta system had started outside India in Persia (Iran) region and in western Asia.
  • The administrative establishment of Iqta was by Iltutmish.
  • Iltutmish started the Iqta system. Meaning of Iqta is- providing land in the form of salary instead of money.
  • Since the time of Balban,  after meeting his and the army’s expenses had to send the surplus revenue to the center. 
  • This surplus amount was called fawazil. This practice was done away by Sikandar Lodhi.

questions.question: Fatwa-i-Alamgiri, a digest of Muslim laws, was written during the period of which of the following kings?
questions.questionHtml: Fatwa-i-Alamgiri, a digest of Muslim laws, was written during the period of which of the following kings?
questions.solution:
Fatwa-i-Alamgiri, a digest of Muslim laws, was written during the period of Aurangzeb.

  • It is a compilation focused on sharia statecraft, general ethics, military strategy, economic policy, justice and punishment which served as the rule and main governing body of the Mughal Empire during the reign of the Mughal emperor Muhammad Muhiuddin Aurangzeb Alamgir.
  • The compilation has been widely regarded as one of Islamic jurisprudence's most well-organized works.
  • The collection includes verses from the Quran, accompanied by accounts from Hadith, including those from Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim, Sunan Abu Dawood, and at-Tirmidhi's Jami.
  • Aurangzeb was the sixth Mughal emperor.

questions.question: The Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque was constructed in around 1197 AD by the sultan of which of the following dynasties of Delhi Sultanate?
questions.questionHtml: The Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque was constructed in around 1197 AD by the sultan of which of the following dynasties of Delhi Sultanate?
questions.solution: The Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque was constructed by Qutb-ud-din Aibak of the Mamluk dynasty around 1193-1197 AD. It was built using remnants of demolished Hindu and Jain temples and is one of the earliest mosques in India. The Mamluk dynasty was the first of the Delhi Sultanate.

questions.question: Who installed the "bell of justice"?
questions.questionHtml: Who installed the "bell of justice"?
questions.solution:
• Jahangir installed the "bell of justice".
  • When he was emperor, he received complaints that Mughal soldiers were kidnapping the women of defeated kingdoms, then he decided to put a bell that is known as the bell of Justice.
  • Therefore soldiers would observe the number of times the bell struck and punished them accordingly.

questions.question: The last Nizam of Hyderabad ________.
questions.questionHtml: The last Nizam of Hyderabad ________.
questions.solution:

  • Nizam

    Description

    Chin Qilich Khan (also known as Nizam ul Mulk and Asaf Jah)
    • Founder of the state of Hyderabad.
    • Founder of Asaf jahi Dynasty

questions.question: The Khalji and Tughluq rulers had appointed military commanders as governors of territories. These lands were called:
questions.questionHtml: The Khalji and Tughluq rulers had appointed military commanders as governors of territories. These lands were called:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Iqta.

Key Points

  • Like the earlier sultans, the Khalji and Tughluq monarchs appointed military commanders as the governors of territories of varying sizes.
  • These lands were called iqta and their holder was called iqtadar or muqti.
  • The duty of the muqtis was to lead military campaigns and maintain law and order in their iqtas.
  • In exchange for their military services, the muqtis collected the revenues of their assignments as salary.
  • They also paid their soldiers from these revenues.
  • Control over muqtis was most effective if their office was not inheritable and if they were assigned Iqtas for a short period before being shifted.

Additional Information

  • Khalji dynasty:
    • It was founded by Jalal-ud-din Khalji who ruled from 1290 to 1296.
    • The Khilji dynasty succeeded the Mamluk Dynasty or the slave dynasty (1206-1290) which was ruled by the early Turkish rulers.
  • Tughluq:
    • Ghiyas-ud-din Tughluq or Ghazi Malik was the founder of the Tughluq dynasty.
    • Tughluq's policy was harsh against Mongols.

questions.question: Whose descendants were the Mughals from their father’s side?
questions.questionHtml: Whose descendants were the Mughals from their father’s side?
questions.solution: Two great lineages of rulers were the ancestors of the Mughals. From their maternal side they were the descendants of Genghis Khan (who died in 1227) who ruled the Mongol tribes, China and Central Asia. From their paternal side they were the descendants of Timur who ruled Iraq, Iran and modern-day Turkey. Timur died in the year 1404. Babar (1526 – 1530) was the first Mughal emperor.

questions.question: Which of the following was NOT a type of sacrifice performed by kings in ancient India to establish their position?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following was NOT a type of sacrifice performed by kings in ancient India to establish their position?
questions.solution:
Muvendavelan was NOT a type of sacrifice performed by kings in ancient India to establish their position.

  • Muvendavelan was a famous military officer of the Chola Empire, known for his generous donation to the numerous temples where he had been deployed by the king.
  • The Rajasuya is connected with the consecration of the King and is prescribed as a way of maintaining the king's sovereignty.
  • It involves a game of throwing dice, in which the king is enthroned and the world is regenerated.
  • Vajapeya Yagna has been performed to preserve peace in the state. It's the highest form of Soma Yajna.
  • Ashvamedha Yagna was performed by the King for fertility and strength in the kingdom.
  • It is a rite of horse sacrifice accompanied by the practice of the Vedic religion of the Shrauta. This has been used by ancient Indian kings to assert their colonial supremacy.

questions.question: This temple, that was built by Raja Bhimdev I of the Solanki Dynasty, has a rectangular pond called ‘Surya Kund’ in front of it. What is the name of this temple?
questions.questionHtml: This temple, that was built by Raja Bhimdev I of the Solanki Dynasty, has a rectangular pond called ‘Surya Kund’ in front of it. What is the name of this temple?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Modhera Sun TempleKey Points

  • The temple with a rectangular pond called “Surya Kund” in front of it is the Modhera Sun Temple, which was built by Raja Bhimdev I of the Solanki Dynasty.
  • The temple is located in Modhera, Gujarat, India.
  • The temple is dedicated to the Hindu sun god, Lord Surya
  • It was built in the early 11th century
  • The temple is designed in the Maru-Gurjara style
  • The temple has a three-tiered structure
  • The temple has intricate carvings
  • The temple has many sculptures of Gods and Goddesses
  • The temple is aligned with the sun during the equinoxes​ 

Additional Information

  • Khajuraho​
    • The Khajuraho Group of Monuments is a group of Hindu temples and Jain temples lo in Chhatarpur district, Madhya Pradesh.
    • They are a World Heritage site by UNESCO. The temples are famous for their architectural symbolism of the nagara-style and their erotic sculptures.
    • Most Khajuraho temples were constructed by the Chandela dynasty between 950 AD and 1050 AD.
    • Historical records mention that by the 12th century, the temple site of Khajuraho had 85 temples, spread over 20 square kilometres.
    • A profusion of sculptures from the surviving temples with intricate details, symbolism and expressiveness of ancient Indian art adorns the Kandariya Mahadeva Temple.
  • Konark Sun Temple
    • Konark Sun Temple was built in 1250 AD.
      • This temple is also called "Black Pagoda".
      • Temple was declared World Heritage Site by UNESCO in 1984.
      • Famous Chandrabhaga Mela took place here every year in the month of February.
      • This temple is attributed to King Narsimhadeva - I of the Eastern Ganga Dynasty.
      • Temple is a classic illustration of Great Kalinga Architecture.
  • Chausath Yogini​
    • Chausath Yogini Temple is devoted to Goddess Durga and the 64 Yoginis who are observed to be her different forms, the Chausath Yogini Temple is constructed with local granite. 
    • The statues of the Yoginis have been arranged circularly and have been carved intricately.
    • The Chausath Yogini Temple, Morena, also popular as Ekattarso Mahadeva Temple, Stands atop an isolated hill approximately a hundred feet high, this circular temple commands a splendid view of the cultivated fields below. 
    • This temple is so famous due to the presence of a multitude of Shivalingas inside its cells.

questions.question: After the Peshwas victory over Shivaji, the capital of Maratha kingdom became ______.
questions.questionHtml: After the Peshwas victory over Shivaji, the capital of Maratha kingdom became ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Poona.

Key Points

  • After the death of Chhatrapati Shivaji in 1680, the Maratha kingdom struggled to hold its own against the Mughals.
  • Shivaji’s sons, Sambhaji was killed by the Mughals in 1689.
  • Sambhaji’s son Shahu was a prisoner in the Mughal camps of Malwa for almost eighteen years before his release in 1708.
  • Even though Shahu did ascend the throne in 1708, from 1713 onwards, it was the Peshwa, Balaji Vishwanath who came to hold the reins of power.
  • Till 1761, when the Marathas were defeated at the hands of the Afghan marauder, Ahmad Shah Abdali, in the Third Battle of Panipat, Peshwas exercised power on the Chattrapati’s behalf.
  • The Chhatrapatis who followed Shahu were reduced to being nominal heads and retired to Satara.
  • The Peshwas held fort at Pune which came to be the real center of power. So, option 4 is correct.
  • The Peshwas were assisted in their military endeavors by various Maratha chiefs — Holkar, Scindia (Shinde), Gaekwad, and Bhonsle — who led roving bands of soldiers that aided the Peshwa army.

questions.question: What fraction of a rupee is one anna, which was a part of the old currency system of India?

questions.solution:

questions.question: Which of the following forts served as a prison for Empress Razia Sultana after she was defeated by her rebellious general, Malik Ikhtiar-ud-din Altunia?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following forts served as a prison for Empress Razia Sultana after she was defeated by her rebellious general, Malik Ikhtiar-ud-din Altunia?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Qila Mubarak.

  • Qila Mubarak fort served as a prison for Empress Razia Sultana after she was defeated by her rebellious general, Malik Ikhtiar-ud-din Altunia.

Key Points

  •  Razia Sultana
    • Born: 1205
    • ​Reign: 1236 – 1240
    • She was Iltutmish’s daughter.
    • She is also the first and last Muslim woman to rule over Delhi.
    • She was defeated by Malik Ikhtiar-ud-din Altunia, the governor of Bathinda.
      • After which sultana was prisoned at Qila Mubarak fort.
    • She later married to Malik Ikhtiar-ud-din Altunia.
    • She was reportedly killed by her brother’s forces.
    • She was succeeded by her brother Muizuddin Bahram Shah.

Additional Information

  • Qila Mubarak Fort - Bathinda, Punjab
  • Gobindgarh Fort - Amritsar, Punjab
  • Shahpur Kandi Fort - Shahpur Kandi, Punjab
  • Anandpur Sahib Fort - Rupnagar, Punjab

questions.question: Who among the following kings founded a suburban township near Vijayanagara called Nagalapuram?
questions.questionHtml: Who among the following kings founded a suburban township near Vijayanagara called Nagalapuram?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Krishnadevaraya.

Key Points

  • Krishnadevaraya:
    • Krishnadevaraya, the ruler of the Vijayanagara Empire, founded the suburban township of Nagalapuram near Vijayanagara.
    • He named the town after his mother, Nagala Devi, as a tribute to her.
    • Krishnadevaraya was one of the greatest rulers of the Vijayanagara Empire, reigning from 1509 to 1529.
    • He was a patron of art, literature, and architecture, and his reign is considered the golden age of the Vijayanagara Empire.
    • Nagalapuram was developed as a cultural and administrative center during his rule.

Additional Information

  • Deva Raya II:
    • Deva Raya II was a prominent ruler of the Vijayanagara Empire who reigned from 1424 to 1446.
    • He is known for his military conquests and administrative reforms.
    • However, he is not associated with the founding of Nagalapuram.
    • His reign is marked by the expansion of the empire and patronage of literature and arts.
    • He is often referred to as one of the most powerful rulers of the Vijayanagara Empire.
  • Rajaraja Chola:
    • Rajaraja Chola I was a great Chola emperor who ruled from 985 to 1014 CE.
    • He is renowned for his military conquests, architectural achievements, and the construction of the Brihadeeswarar Temple in Thanjavur.
    • His reign marked the peak of the Chola Empire's power and influence.
    • However, he belonged to the Chola dynasty and is not connected to the Vijayanagara Empire or Nagalapuram.
    • His contributions were primarily in South India, particularly in Tamil Nadu.
  • Rajendra I:
    • Rajendra Chola I, the son of Rajaraja Chola, ruled from 1014 to 1044 CE.
    • He expanded the Chola Empire to its greatest extent, including parts of Southeast Asia.
    • He is known for his naval expeditions and the construction of the city of Gangaikonda Cholapuram.
    • Like Rajaraja Chola, he belonged to the Chola dynasty and is unrelated to the Vijayanagara Empire or Nagalapuram.
    • His reign is celebrated for its military and cultural achievements.

questions.question: The Battle of Karnal is known for the invasion of which of the following aggressors against India?
questions.questionHtml: The Battle of Karnal is known for the invasion of which of the following aggressors against India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Nadir Shah.

Key Points

  • The Battle of Karnal occurred in 1739, when Nadir Shah, the ruler of the Afsharid dynasty of Persia, invaded India.
  • He defeated the Mughal army led by Muhammad Shah at Karnal and subsequently sacked Delhi, the Mughal capital.
  • This decisive victory marked the beginning of the decline of the Mughal Empire.
  • Afsharid Dynasty:
    • The Turkoman Afshar tribe in Iran's northeastern area of Khorasan gave rise to the Afsharid dynasty, which controlled Iran (Persia) in the middle of the eighteenth century.
    • Nadir Shah (Nader Shah Afshar), a brilliant military tactician who deposed the final Safavid dynasty member and crowned himself Shah of Iran, founded the dynasty in 1736.
    • Under Nader's leadership, Iran reached its widest point since the Sasanian Empire.
    • At its height, it controlled portions of Iraq, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, and Oman in addition to modern-day Iran, Armenia, Georgia, the Azerbaijan Republic, Afghanistan, Bahrain, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, and Pakistan, as well as portions of the North Caucasus (Dagestan).

Additional Information

  • Ahmed Shah Abdali:
    • The founder of the Durrani Empire and the modern state of Afghanistan was Ahmad Shah Abdali, sometimes referred to as Ahmad Khan Abdali or Ahmad Shah Durrani.
    • After Nadir Shah passed away in 1747, Abdali was selected to take over and attacked India on several occasions between 1748 and 1767.
    • During this period, he launched eight invasions of India, conquered Punjab, and defeated the Marathas in the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761.
  • Shah Shuja:
    • The second child of Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan and Empress Mumtaz Mahal was Mirza Shah Shuja.
    • He served as governor of both Bengal and Odisha; his capital was Dhaka.
    • Following Shah Jahan's sickness in September of 1657, the brothers had a power struggle.
    • Shah Shuja declared himself to be the Emperor, but Aurangzeb took the Dehli throne and dispatched Mir Jumla to bring Shuja under control.
    • On January 5, 1659, Shuja lost the Battle of Khajwa.
  • Nasir Khan:
    • While Nasir Khan participated in rebellions against the Mughal Empire, he wasn't involved in the Battle of Karnal.

questions.question: Alha and Udal, who gave stiff resistance to the enemy, belonged to which of the following Rajput States?

Key Points

  • Their bravery and resistance against enemies are celebrated in the epic ballad Alha-Khand.
  • They were born to Chandravanshiya Kshatriya family. Udal was 12 years younger than Alha.
  • They learned the art of war and religious knowledge from their guru, Gorakhnath.
  • Alha and Udal were the learned scholars who shared a long-lasting bond between them. They were known for their bravery, serving their religion and love for their motherland.

Additional Information

  • Chandela dynasty:
    • ​They dominated Madhya Pradesh's eastern region (Area of Bundelkhand) with capital city is Mohoba, Khajuraho.
    • They were one among the 36 Rajput clans .
    • Under the early monarchs like Jayashakti Dhanga, who was a renowned leader of this dynasty, the Chandella kingdom gradually grew.
      • He adopted the name Maharajadhiraja.
      • His battles against Mahmud of Ghazni are widely recognized.
      • During his rule, a number of the Khajuraho temples were constructed.
  • Paramara dynasty:
    • In west-central India, the Paramara dynasty dominated Malwa and the surrounding areas from the ninth to the fourteenth centuries.
    • Upendra, also known as Krishnaraja, was the Malwa region's founder of the Parmar dynasty.
    • It was situated in the early ninth century, north of the Narmada River.
  • Kalachuri dynasty:
    • It was a strong dynasty that governed Central India.
    • It had two branches that governed in distinct locations for various ages.
      • The Kalachuri Dynasty of Mahismati was the name given to the previous government.
        • Between the sixth and seventh centuries AD, they ruled across west-central India.

  • Gahadavala dynasty:
    • ​The Gahadavala dynasty emerged as a Rajput state in the eleventh and twelfth centuries.
    • It ruled over parts of what are now the states of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar in modern India.
    • Another name for it was the Gahadavalas of Kannauj.
    • It expanded upto Delhi.
    • In the east, it reached Patna and the Munger districts of Bihar.
    • The reign of Govinchandra was the pinnacle of the dynasty's power.  

    • In the latter part of the 12th century A.D., they were overthrown by Muhammad of Ghur's assaults.

questions.question: In medieval architecture, Sarais are places used for _________.
questions.questionHtml: In medieval architecture, Sarais are places used for _________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is temporary accommodation.

Key Points

  • Sarais were essentially inns or rest houses established in medieval times.
  • They provided temporary accommodation for travelers, merchants, and pilgrims.
  • These structures were often found along trade routes and were crucial for the safety and comfort of travelers.
  • Sarais typically included facilities like rooms for sleeping, stables for animals, and sometimes even food provisions.

Additional Information

  • Medieval Architecture
    • Medieval architecture refers to the architectural styles that were prevalent in Europe during the Middle Ages, roughly from the 5th to the late 15th century.
    • It includes a variety of styles such as Romanesque, Gothic, and Byzantine.
    • Key features of medieval architecture include the use of stone, pointed arches, ribbed vaults, and flying buttresses.
    • Buildings from this period include castles, churches, and fortifications, all serving different purposes from defense to religious worship.
  • Trade Routes
    • Trade routes were essential pathways used for the commercial movement of goods and services.
    • They facilitated the exchange of commodities like spices, silk, precious metals, and other goods between different regions.
    • Famous medieval trade routes include the Silk Road, the Amber Road, and the Trans-Saharan trade routes.
    • These routes not only boosted economic activity but also enabled cultural and technological exchanges between civilizations.
  • Hospices and Inns
    • Similar to sarais, hospices and inns were established to offer lodging and care for travelers and pilgrims.
    • Hospices, often run by religious institutions, provided free or low-cost shelter and food to the needy and the sick.
    • Inns were more commercial establishments that charged for lodging and meals, catering mainly to merchants and other travelers.
    • These facilities played a significant role in medieval society by promoting travel and commerce.

questions.question: The policy of Permanent Settlement was introduced in India in ____.
questions.questionHtml: The policy of Permanent Settlement was introduced in India in ____.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 1793.

Key Points

  • The Permanent Settlement, also known as the Zamindari System, was introduced in Bengal by the East India Company under Lord Cornwallis in 1793.
  • The system was designed as a legal regime to stabilize property ownership and encourage the landowning Zamindars to improve the agricultural productivity of the lands they governed over.
  • Its key feature was the fixing of tax obligations in perpetuity.
  • The taxation rights were given to Zamindars, who were expected to collect these taxes from the peasant communities that resided on the land.

 Additional Information

  • The Permanent Settlement was first introduced in Bengal and Bihar and later expanded to Varanasi and the south district of Madras.
  • It eventually spread all over northern India courtesy of a series of regulations promulgated on 1st May 1793.
  • These regulations persisted until the Charter Act of 1833 came to hold.
  • The Permanent Settlement marked a significant chapter in the economic and social history of colonial India, shaping the contours of social power and land relations in regions it was introduced.

questions.question: Who signed the treaty of Alinagar with the British?

questions.solution:
Siraj-ud-Daula signed the treaty of Alinagar with the British.

questions.question: Which of the following was the last dynasty to rule over Gujarat before it passed on to the hands of Ala-ud-din Khilji, Sultan of Delhi?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following was the last dynasty to rule over Gujarat before it passed on to the hands of Ala-ud-din Khilji, Sultan of Delhi?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Vaghela Dynasty.

Key Points

  • Vaghela Dynasty
    • It was the last dynasty to rule over Gujarat before it passed on to the hands of Ala-ud-din Khilji, Sultan of Delhi.
    • The Vaghela dynasty was a short-lived dynasty that ruled Gujarat from its capital of Dholka in the 13th century CE.
    • The Vaghelas was the last Hindu monarchs to rule large parts of Gujarat, before the Muslim conquest of the region.
    • Capital: Dhavalakka (modern Dholka)
    • Common languages: Apabhramsa, Old Gujarati, Prakrit.

Additional Information

  • In 1299, the Delhi Sultanate ruler Alauddin Khalji sent an army to ransack the Gujarat region of India, which was ruled by the Vaghela king Karna.
  • The Delhi forces plundered several major cities of Gujarat, including Anahilavada (Patan), Khambhat, Surat, and Somnath.
  • Karna was able to regain control of at least a part of his kingdom in the later years.
  • However, in 1304, a second invasion by Alauddin's forces permanently ended the Vaghela dynasty and resulted in the annexation of Gujarat to the Delhi Sultanate.

questions.question: Indra Sawhney and others vs UOI case is related to?
questions.questionHtml: Indra Sawhney and others vs UOI case is related to?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Reservation.

 

Indra Sawhney v. Union of India 1992:

  • At the beginning of the 1990s, the central government implemented the Mandal Commission recommendations for reservation of other backward classes.
  • This created chaos in various sections of the society.
  • Consequently, a PIL was filed, and resulted in one of the most significant judgments namely “Indra Sawhney case”.
  • Also known as Mandal Case.
  • Became the cornerstone in the present reservation structure of the country. So, option 2 is correct.

Salient features of Indra Sawhney judgment:

  • It recognized socially and economically backward classes as a category and recognized the validity of the 27 percent reservation.
  • The concept of the ‘creamy layer’ gained currency through this judgment.
  • Those among the OBCs who had transcended their social backwardness were to be excluded from the reservation.
  • It laid down a 50 percent limit on reservations and observed that economic, social, and educational criteria were needed to define backward classes.
  • Reservation for backward classes (which include OBCs and SCs & STs) should be confined to initial appointments and not extend to promotions.

questions.question: What was the revenue system during Mughal emperor Akbar’s reign called?
questions.questionHtml: What was the revenue system during Mughal emperor Akbar’s reign called?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is  Zabt System.

Key Points

  • The revenue system during Akbar’s reign was called Zabt System.
  • Raja Todar Mal was Akbar's finance minister, he introduced this system.
  • He took a careful survey of crop yields and prices cultivated for a 10 years period 1570-1580.
  • The system of taxation was called Dahshala.
  • In this system, each province was divided into revenue circles with their own rates of revenue for each crop.
  • On this basis, the tax was fixed on each crop in cash.

Additional Information

  • Akbar was one of the mightiest emperors during the Mughal Era.
  • He was born in October 1542 and died on 27th October 1605.
  • Akbar was the third Mughal Emperor.
  • His reign was between 1556-1605 AD.
  • He was crowned in 1556, at the young age of thirteen years.
  • He was assisted by Barram Khan.
  • He is known for his liberal religious policies, relationship with Indian kings, conquests, etc.
  • In 1564, he abolished the jizyah tax levied on non-muslims.
  • Akbar introduced Mansabdari System in his administration.

questions.question: When was the Battle of Tukaroi fought where Akbar defeated Sultanate of Bengal and Bihar?

questions.solution: The correct answer is 1575. The Battle of Tukaroi was fought on March 3, 1575, between the Mughal Empire led by Akbar and the Sultanate of Bengal and Bihar led by Daud Khan Karrani. It was a significant battle in the history of medieval India, as it marked the beginning of the end of the Karrani dynasty's rule in Bengal and Bihar.
